about: The Lord's Prayer, which Jesus taught His disciples (Mt 6:9–13 and Lk 11:2–4). It addresses God as Father. It asks that His name be hallowed, His kingdom come, and His will be done, and then asks for daily bread, forgiveness, protection in temptation, and deliverance from evil.

s01.translation: Our Father, who art in heaven,

s04.translation: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

s05.translation: Give us this day our daily bread.

s06.translation: And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

s07.translation: And lead us not into temptation,

s08.translation: but deliver us from evil. Amen.

w002.function: Agrees with “Pater” (w001). The plural expresses a common prayer.

w004.function: After the vocative the relative clause keeps the 2nd person: “who art”, not “who is”.

w006.function: Plural, while “cælo” (w018) later in the prayer is singular. The received English renders both as singular.

w013.function: A subjunctive expressing a petition. The same form “fiat” occurs in Mary's reply at the Annunciation (Lk 1:38).

w030.function: Dative denoting the person whose debts are forgiven.

w035.function: The subject spelled out for emphasis.

w036.function: Indicative within the clause introduced by “sicut” (w033).

w037.function: We forgive whom — the debtors. Literally “to the debtors”, traditionally “those who trespass against us”.

w040.function: With the subjunctive “indúcas” (w042) it forms a negative petition: “that Thou not…”.

w042.function: Subjunctive after “ne” (w040) — the negation rides on “ne”. The received English joins them as “lead us not”.

w043.function: With the accusative — direction: “into temptation”. Compare “in” (w005) with the ablative — place.

w045.function: The petition turns: not into temptation, but toward deliverance.

w046.function: The last of the prayer's three imperatives: “da” (w025), “dimítte” (w029), líbera.

w049.function: The form leaves the gender open: neuter “malum” (evil) or masculine “malus” (the Evil One)? The tradition reads both senses at once. The embolism just after the prayer — “Líbera nos ab ómnibus malis” — takes the word up in the neuter plural.
